title: Tree-sitter Trial
eyebrow: Trial results · the code map for the docs context layer (#306)

short.lead: I ran tree-sitter on three of your projects: PlunderSpell's own 544 C# scripts, this repo's Python and pages, and focus-deck-app's JavaScript, HTML and CSS. All three projects together took 1.0 second. Every definition I counted by hand was found, 66 of 66. References needed two query fixes, one for C# and one for HTML. After those, every hand-counted reference was found. Two limits remain, and each needs your decision. The full write-up is in docs/trials/2026-10-18-tree-sitter/README.md on the branch AjsAgent/docs-context-layer.
short.hint: Tap a row to see what was measured.
items: Parse and query time: 0.53 s for 544 C# files, 0.18 s for 26 Python files, 0.09 s for 55 pages, 0.02 s for 14 JavaScript files. Parsing a single file takes 0.12 s, including Python's start-up time. Both full runs gave identical counts.

Three files per language, read and counted by hand. C# references were 14 of 21 at first: null-safe calls such as previous?.Exit() and event subscriptions such as onChanged += OnReplicated were missed. One query line fixed each, and the recount was 21 of 21. The HTML query also missed the page's script tag at first; one fix covered that.
Names alone can't say which Update a call reaches

tree-sitter reads syntax, not types. In PlunderSpell, 25% of references match more than one definition, such as Update in 55 classes and Awake in 54. Another 48% are Unity or .NET calls with no definition in the project. A dependency line built from names alone could point at the wrong class.

The package ships without grammars. It downloaded 7 of them, 12 MB, the first time each language was used. It never printed the address it downloaded from, and the address is not in its files. A new machine needs the network once, or the install has to fetch them up front.

TypeScript, because no project here uses it. The third Python file. CSS beyond its first 45 lines. macOS and Linux. JavaScript inside a page's own script tag is skipped; the house-rules pages are built that way, so the build should read those script tags as JavaScript.

choices: names
How should a dependency line handle a name that several classes define?
A
List every match and mark the line as ambiguous
Nothing is guessed. A doc says "calls Update (55 definitions)", and the session checks the code only for that line. Works the same in every language.
B
Add a C#-only pass with Roslyn, the C# compiler, to resolve types
Exact links in C#, the language with the most ambiguity. It brings back the dotnet runtime that the parser choice avoided. It would also make C# refreshes slower, but I haven't timed that.
C
Use A now, and open an issue to try Roslyn later if ambiguous lines get in the way
A ships first, and the Roslyn idea is kept with evidence of how often it matters.
In every option, references with no definition in the project, such as Unity and .NET calls, are left out of the dependency lines.
grammars
How should a machine get the grammars?
A
The install step downloads the six grammars up front and says so
One network fetch at install, never in the middle of a session. The install fails loudly if the download fails.
B
Ship the grammar files inside the plugin
No download at all. Adds 12 MB to the plugin on Windows, measured; other platforms not measured, and every grammar update means a plugin release.
Either way, finding the download address and testing an offline machine comes first.

wrapup.summary: tree-sitter is fast. It found every hand-counted definition and, after two query fixes, every hand-counted reference. Name ambiguity and the grammar download need your call.
wrapup.changing: Nothing in the plugin. The trial script, its output and the write-up are on the branch AjsAgent/docs-context-layer.
wrapup.blocking: Your answers to the two choices.
wrapup.next: Your answers join the list on issue #306 for the grilling session, and I log them in the decisions log.
